extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scholars, Ph.D. candidates and graduate students in entrepreneurship (and related) domains
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting, and reporting standalone systematic literature reviews (SLRs) in the field of entrepreneurship, with field-specific recommendations (databases, journal-quality thresholds, synthesis expectations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the need for an SLR / specify a research question
rubrics_metrics.description: An SLR is created around a research question that it tries to answer. Authors must ask if and why an SLR is needed or if a traditional review is adequate; specify a research question and determine whether sufficient literature exists to justify a synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for existing SLRs via initial searches (e.g., Google Scholar), decide whether existing reviews leave room for new questions or are poorly done. SLRs are suitable to answer state-of-the-art questions, identify gaps, develop theoretical constructs, or map a field; avoid SLRs when the question is not detailed/suitable or when recent good SLRs already exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a transparent review protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a review protocol at the beginning that outlines the whole process: search strings, databases, inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality criteria, data extraction items, and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protocol is essential for objectivity and reproducibility. Treat it as adaptable (do not consider it set in stone) but document and report every change. The protocol should be the basis for the extraction sheet and subsequent steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and report transparency details (dates, counts, protocol changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be transparent: note the date you searched, record the number of articles found in each database, and document any changes to the protocol or extraction sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a transparent and objective process; changes must be noted. This supports reproducibility and defends against criticisms of subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple academic databases (prefer peer-reviewed journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct searches across several major online academic databases (e.g., ABI Inform/ProQuest, EBSCO/Business Source, JSTOR, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always use more than one database (use as many as accessible) to cover literature comprehensively. For Entrepreneurship, concentrate on academic journal articles as the primary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Google Scholar as primary search source
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use Google Scholar as the primary reproducible search system for the SLR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Google Scholar is not reproducible (personalized algorithmic results) and includes many non-academic sources; it can be used to find full texts or grey literature cross-checks but not as the primary search database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define keywords and search strings; iteratively refine
rubrics_metrics.description: Define keywords and search strings including synonyms and related terms; pilot searches and refine strings based on initial results and cross-reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult experts to identify synonyms (e.g., 'corporate entrepreneurship' vs 'intrapreneurship'), perform initial short searches to detect missing keywords, and adapt search strings to the intended breadth or depth of the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide search scope: title vs abstract vs full text
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to search only in titles, titles+abstracts, or whole texts based on the review's breadth/depth goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title-only searches may suffice if they yield enough literature; expand to abstracts if more coverage is needed. Searching full text may uncover loosely related papers but is less recommended for reproducibility and may bring many irrelevant hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and apply quality thresholds using journal rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established journal rankings (VHB JQ3, ABS, JCR IF) to set transparent quality thresholds for included studies (recommendation: include journals rated 'C' or higher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust the three main journal rankings rather than rating publications subjectively. Use the conversion table provided to map rankings and transparently exclude low-ranked outlets; allow exceptions only with strong justification and deep evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer peer-reviewed journal articles; exclude grey literature by default
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate on academic, peer-reviewed journal articles for Entrepreneurship SLRs; grey literature (working papers, conference proceedings) is discouraged as primary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grey literature complicates reproducibility and quality assurance. If grey literature must be included, provide careful justification and deep evaluation, acknowledging potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening process: staged selection (title -> abstract -> full text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a staged screening: first filter by title, then abstract, then full-text reading to exclude irrelevant or low-quality papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the title suffices to exclude irrelevant studies; abstract screening refines selection for focused/narrow questions. Use the staged approach to manage volume and ensure relevance to the protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document eliminated studies and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a transparent protocol of eliminated studies with reasons for exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report which studies were eliminated and why (e.g., failed quality threshold, not relevant to the research question) to support reproducibility and defend choices to reviewers/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a systematic data extraction form/sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Design an extraction sheet (e.g., in Excel) based on the protocol to record all items to be extracted from included studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify extraction fields at the start, adapt if necessary (but record changes). The sheet enforces consistency and supports later synthesis and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple coders/authors for data extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce bias and extraction errors, involve more than one author in the data extraction process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple reviewers help prevent 'data extraction bias' and missing important data. Document who extracted what and reconcile disagreements systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct quality appraisal of included studies (objective criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess study quality using transparent, objective criteria—prefer using journal rankings rather than subjective, per-article scoring by the review authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, supplement journal-ranking thresholds with deeper quality checks for borderline cases or highly relevant but lower-ranked works; explain and document any exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize data focusing on concepts, not authors
rubrics_metrics.description: In the synthesis, prioritize conceptual mapping and thematic/conceptual integration rather than author-by-author summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pure summary of content—synthesis should distill concepts, highlight patterns, irregular results, methodological differences, and lead to conclusions and research gaps. Use tables and figures to present synthesized results (this section is a common cause of desk rejections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tables, figures and knowledge maps in synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilize visual tools (tables, figures, knowledge maps) to present synthesis and structure findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge maps help identify major literature, trends, and niches, and support development of theoretical constructs. They also help readers and the author to define research focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance breadth and depth depending on literature volume and heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose breadth vs depth based on the amount and heterogeneity of available literature and the research question's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields with abundant, fragmented literature may benefit from broader mapping; nascent fields or narrow questions may require exhaustive inclusion or deep focus. Decide whether to include qualitative vs quantitative studies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update the database search before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-run database searches for new literature shortly before manuscript submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the review captures the most recent relevant studies; note the date of the final search in the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report limitations and acknowledge residual author bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state limitations of the SLR, including remaining author subjectivity and possible biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with transparency, authors are not completely objective; discuss limitations in study selection, extraction, and synthesis stages, and how they might affect conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rate publications subjectively; rely on transparent external metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ad-hoc subjective rating of individual publications; instead, rely on transparent metrics like established journal rankings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including lower-ranked but important articles, provide clear rationale and deeper evaluation rather than subjective numeric ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider use of software/algorithms/NLP but ensure transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Software and automated algorithms (e.g., NLP) can analyze larger volumes of literature but must be applied transparently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If analytic algorithms are used, make code/algorithms available (e.g., GitHub) and use consistent algorithms across time to support reproducibility. Be aware that opaque automated methods can undermine transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the SLR contributes (definitions, frameworks, gaps, theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for contribution-focused outputs: create clear definitions, synthesize literature, assess methodologies/results, identify irregular findings, develop frameworks, and highlight future research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-quality SLR should consolidate fragmented terminology, map current perspectives, support theory development, and explicitly identify research gaps and potential fruitful directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the staged SLR process (planning; identifying/evaluating; extracting/synthesizing; disseminating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to the general process stages: planning the review (identify need, develop protocol), identifying and evaluating studies, extracting and synthesizing data, and disseminating findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stages as an organizing framework; adapt steps for the specific review but document adherence and deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target appropriate journals and check exemplar SLRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult highly-ranked journals and journals specializing in review articles to set quality expectations and target outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine best-practice SLRs in the field (examples provided) to guide structure and expectations. Note that review-specialized journals and special review issues may be appropriate targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about inclusion when niche literature is sparse
rubrics_metrics.description: If the topic is extremely narrow or literature is scarce, avoid claiming a standalone SLR unless the review can still produce novel synthesis; alternatively include all identified sources or choose a different methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In nascent fields with few papers, exhaustive analysis might be necessary; however, a very limited literature base rarely justifies a standalone SLR unless it can produce new insights or theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record full-text access attempts and retrieval methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When full texts are not accessible in searched databases, document efforts to retrieve them (e.g., ResearchGate, contacting authors, colleague access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how inaccessible but relevant papers were handled, and which retrieval channels were used. This supports transparency about potential sampling limitations.
